Stage 5 — Reduced-order models of the flow fields and a latent-space design search¶

Vamsi Gudipati

This notebook builds two reduced-order models of the AirfRANS flow fields of four-digit NACA airfoils on a regular grid: a linear one from proper orthogonal decomposition with eight modes and a nonlinear one from a β-variational autoencoder with eight latent coordinates. I then train a surrogate from the airfoil parameters and operating conditions to the latent coordinates and an aerodynamic head from the latent coordinates to lift and drag, chain them, search a grid of candidate airfoils for the best lift-to-drag ratio, and answer eight questions about the models. Four extra sections look at the spread of an ensemble of chains over the design space, what the latent coordinates encode, the cost of a query, and where the chain would sit in a design workflow. Wherever a result depends on a random initialisation I repeat it with three seeds.

Portfolio page: https://vamsigudipati.github.io/airfoil-rom-betavae-design.html

AirfRANS: ROM, beta-VAE and aerodynamic design¶

This notebook starts a practical project using the interpolated AirfRANS simulations for four-digit NACA-family airfoils.

The complete workflow is:

  1. Load and inspect the prepared database.
  2. Visualize two-dimensional RANS fields.
  3. Construct a linear ROM using POD/PCA.
  4. Construct a nonlinear ROM using a beta-VAE.
  5. Compare both representations at the same latent dimension.
  6. Learn a surrogate from NACA parameters and operating conditions to the latent space.
  7. Connect the latent representation to lift and drag.
  8. Search for an efficient airfoil and generate its predicted polar.

The first sections are ready to execute. Later sections provide the initial implementation and the structure for the project.

5. Prepare the fields for reduced-order modeling¶

Each channel is standardized using training statistics only. The same transformation is applied to the test set. The statistics are retained to recover dimensional or nondimensional physical fields later.

channel_std = train_fields.std(axis=(0, 2, 3), keepdims=True)
channel_std = np.maximum(channel_std, 1.0e-8)

train_scaled = (train_fields - channel_mean) / channel_std
test_scaled = (test_fields - channel_mean) / channel_std

6. Linear ROM: POD/PCA¶

POD treats each complete multichannel field as one snapshot. The first comparison will use eight latent coordinates for both POD and the beta-VAE.

In [9]:
LATENT_DIM = 8

train_snapshots = train_scaled.reshape(train_scaled.shape[0], -1)
test_snapshots = test_scaled.reshape(test_scaled.shape[0], -1)

pod = PCA(
    n_components=LATENT_DIM,
    svd_solver="randomized",
    random_state=SEED
)

z_pod_train = pod.fit_transform(train_snapshots)
z_pod_test = pod.transform(test_snapshots)

pod_test_reconstruction = pod.inverse_transform(z_pod_test)
pod_test_reconstruction = pod_test_reconstruction.reshape(test_scaled.shape)

pod_test_mse = np.mean((test_scaled - pod_test_reconstruction) ** 2)

print("POD latent shape:", z_pod_train.shape)
print("Explained variance:", pod.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())
print("Standardized test MSE:", pod_test_mse)

7. Nonlinear ROM: beta-VAE¶

The beta-VAE uses the same latent dimension as POD. Its loss combines reconstruction and regularization:

loss = reconstruction_loss + beta * KL_loss.

A beta warm-up is used to reduce the risk of posterior collapse.

In [12]:
class Sampling(layers.Layer):
    def call(self, inputs):
        mu, logvar = inputs
        epsilon = tf.random.normal(shape=tf.shape(mu))
        return mu + tf.exp(0.5 * logvar) * epsilon


def build_beta_vae(input_shape, latent_dim):
    encoder_input = keras.Input(shape=input_shape, name="field")

    x = layers.Conv2D(16, 4, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(encoder_input)
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, 4, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, 4, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)

    encoded_shape = tuple(int(value) for value in x.shape[1:])
    x = layers.Flatten()(x)

    mu = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name="mu")(x)
    logvar = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name="logvar")(x)
    z = Sampling(name="sampling")([mu, logvar])

    encoder = keras.Model(
        encoder_input, [mu, logvar, z], name="encoder"
    )

    decoder_input = keras.Input(shape=(latent_dim,), name="latent_vector")
    x = layers.Dense(int(np.prod(encoded_shape)), activation="relu")(decoder_input)
    x = layers.Reshape(encoded_shape)(x)
    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(32, 4, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)
    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(16, 4, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)
    decoder_output = layers.Conv2DTranspose(
        input_shape[-1], 4, strides=2, padding="same", name="reconstruction"
    )(x)

    decoder = keras.Model(decoder_input, decoder_output, name="decoder")
    return encoder, decoder


def beta_vae_loss(reconstruction, target, mu, logvar, beta):
    reconstruction_loss = tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(reconstruction - target))
    kl_loss = -0.5 * tf.reduce_mean(
        1.0 + logvar - tf.square(mu) - tf.exp(logvar)
    )
    total_loss = reconstruction_loss + beta * kl_loss
    return total_loss, reconstruction_loss, kl_loss
In [13]:
BATCH_SIZE = 32
N_EPOCHS = 100
LEARNING_RATE = 1.0e-3
BETA_MAX = 1.0e-3
BETA_WARMUP_EPOCHS = 30

# TensorFlow/Keras uses channels-last images: (N, NY, NX, channels).
train_images = np.transpose(train_scaled, (0, 2, 3, 1)).astype(np.float32)
test_images = np.transpose(test_scaled, (0, 2, 3, 1)).astype(np.float32)

train_dataset = (
    tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(train_images)
    .shuffle(len(train_images), seed=SEED, reshuffle_each_iteration=True)
    .batch(BATCH_SIZE)
    .prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
)

encoder, decoder = build_beta_vae(
    input_shape=train_images.shape[1:], latent_dim=LATENT_DIM
)

optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)
history = {"total": [], "reconstruction": [], "kl": []}

# --- snapshots of one fixed test case for the animation (the case is fixed before training; nothing is tuned on it) ---
# mu is read through a mu-only model, which never calls the Sampling layer, so no random number is consumed
# and the training sequence is the same as without the snapshots.
ANIM_CASE = 0          # declared evaluation case: test case 0, the case of cells 20 and 26 (there is no validation set)
ANIM_EVERY = 2
mu_model = keras.Model(encoder.input, encoder.get_layer("mu").output)
anim_snapshots = []

def take_snapshot(epoch, beta_value):
    rec_case = decoder(mu_model(test_images[ANIM_CASE:ANIM_CASE + 1], training=False), training=False).numpy()[0]
    rec_all = decoder.predict(mu_model.predict(test_images, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0), batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0)
    anim_snapshots.append({"epoch": epoch, "beta": beta_value, "recon": rec_case,
                           "test_mse": float(np.mean((rec_all - test_images) ** 2)),
                           "history": {k: list(v) for k, v in history.items()}})

take_snapshot(0, 0.0)
# --- end of the animation lines ---

for epoch in range(N_EPOCHS):
    accumulated = np.zeros(3, dtype=float)
    beta = BETA_MAX * min(1.0, (epoch + 1) / BETA_WARMUP_EPOCHS)

    for batch in train_dataset:
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            mu, logvar, z = encoder(batch, training=True)
            reconstruction = decoder(z, training=True)
            total, reconstruction_loss, kl_loss = beta_vae_loss(
                reconstruction, batch, mu, logvar, beta
            )

        trainable_variables = (
            encoder.trainable_variables + decoder.trainable_variables
        )
        gradients = tape.gradient(total, trainable_variables)
        optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, trainable_variables))

        accumulated += [
            float(total), float(reconstruction_loss), float(kl_loss)
        ]

    accumulated /= len(train_dataset)
    history["total"].append(accumulated[0])
    history["reconstruction"].append(accumulated[1])
    history["kl"].append(accumulated[2])

    if epoch == 0 or (epoch + 1) % ANIM_EVERY == 0:   # record a snapshot for the animation
        take_snapshot(epoch + 1, beta)

    if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0 or epoch == 0:
        print(
            f"Epoch {epoch + 1:3d} | beta={beta:.2e} | "
            f"reconstruction={accumulated[1]:.4e} | "
            f"KL={accumulated[2]:.4e}"
        )

9. Next stage: surrogate to the latent space¶

The next model will learn the mapping

(m, p, t, log(Re), alpha) -> latent vector.

Two targets can be compared:

  • POD coordinates z_pod_train.
  • beta-VAE posterior means mu_train.

The posterior mean, rather than a random latent sample, should be used as the deterministic target.

In [16]:
mu_train, _, _ = encoder.predict(
    train_images, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0
)
mu_test, _, _ = encoder.predict(
    test_images, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0
)

z_vae_train = mu_train.astype(np.float32)
z_vae_test = mu_test.astype(np.float32)

def prepare_parameters(parameters):
    prepared = parameters.copy().astype(np.float32)
    prepared[:, 3] = np.log10(prepared[:, 3])
    return prepared

parameter_scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = parameter_scaler.fit_transform(
    prepare_parameters(train_parameters)
).astype(np.float32)
X_test = parameter_scaler.transform(
    prepare_parameters(test_parameters)
).astype(np.float32)

print("Surrogate input shape:", X_train.shape)
print("POD latent target:    ", z_pod_train.shape)
print("VAE latent target:    ", z_vae_train.shape)

In [17]:
def build_latent_surrogate(parameter_dim, latent_dim):
    return keras.Sequential(
        [
            keras.Input(shape=(parameter_dim,)),
            layers.Dense(64, activation="tanh"),
            layers.Dense(64, activation="tanh"),
            layers.Dense(latent_dim),
        ],
        name="latent_surrogate",
    )


latent_surrogate = build_latent_surrogate(
    parameter_dim=X_train.shape[1], latent_dim=LATENT_DIM
)
latent_surrogate.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1.0e-3), loss="mse"
)

11. Aerodynamic head and optimization plan¶

Once latent coordinates and force coefficients are available, train a small model:

latent vector -> (CL, CD).

The complete differentiable chain becomes:

(m, p, t, Re, alpha) -> latent surrogate -> latent vector -> aerodynamic head -> (CL, CD).

A practical design problem is:

  • Fix Reynolds number.
  • Generate many admissible four-digit NACA candidates.
  • Predict CL and CD.
  • Maximize CL/CD, or minimize CD subject to CL being above a prescribed value.
  • Decode the latent field of the selected design.
  • Vary alpha to construct its predicted polar.

Directly optimizing a free latent vector is left as an extension because the resulting point may not correspond to a realizable NACA geometry.

In [19]:
def build_aerodynamic_head(latent_dim):
    return keras.Sequential(
        [
            keras.Input(shape=(latent_dim,)),
            layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh"),
            layers.Dense(2),
        ],
        name="aerodynamic_head",
    )


aerodynamic_head = build_aerodynamic_head(LATENT_DIM)
aerodynamic_head.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1.0e-3), loss="mse"
)


# Tasks:
# 1. Train this network using CL and CD.
# 2. Evaluate MAE and R2 separately for CL and CD.
# 3. Create a candidate set of (m, p, t, Re, alpha).
# 4. Find the candidate with maximum CL/CD.
# 5. Generate CL(alpha), CD(alpha), and the drag polar.

12. Proposed questions for the project¶

  1. How many POD modes are needed to retain 95% and 99% of the snapshot variance?
  2. At the same latent dimension, which method reconstructs unseen fields more accurately: POD or beta-VAE?
  3. Which variables and spatial regions are most difficult to reconstruct?
  4. How much error is caused by dimensionality reduction and how much by the latent surrogate?
  5. Can the latent representation predict CL and CD accurately enough for design screening?
  6. Which admissible NACA four-digit-family design maximizes CL/CD at a selected Reynolds number and angle of attack?
  7. What does the predicted polar of the selected design look like?
  8. Does the optimum lie close to the training distribution, or is the surrogate being extrapolated?

13. Suggested division of work¶

Core work¶

  • Load and visualize the database.
  • Train and evaluate POD.
  • Train and evaluate the beta-VAE.
  • Compare both ROMs.
  • Train one latent surrogate.

If time permits¶

  • Predict CL and CD from the latent representation.
  • Search for a high-efficiency airfoil.
  • Generate its predicted polar.
  • Study out-of-distribution behavior and latent-space interpolation.

Part B — The two open tasks¶

In this part I complete the two tasks the notebook leaves open, the latent surrogate of cell 30 and the aerodynamic head of cell 34, and I add a training animation of the β-VAE with three analysis questions (A1–A3). What matters here is the split of the reconstruction error into a reduction part and a surrogate part (cell 46), and the test scores of the complete chain against the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3 (cell 48). Cell 24 also records animation snapshots, without changing the training. I save the fitted objects in ../models/05_airfrans_rom_betavae_design/, the tables and figures in ../results/05_airfrans_rom_betavae_design/ and the animation in ../animations/.

Animation — the β-VAE learning the pressure field¶

I recorded snapshots during the training of cell 24 on one fixed case chosen in advance: test case 0, the case already plotted in cells 21 and 27, since the notebook has no validation set. I fixed the case before training and did not tune anything on its curve.

  • Top-left — reconstruction of the scaled pressure field of that case, decoded from the posterior mean μ at the current epoch.
  • Top-right — losses: reconstruction and KL terms per epoch (log scale), with β on a second axis.
  • Bottom-left — error of that reconstruction against the reference field, with the airfoil outline (zero level of the signed distance).
  • Bottom-right — standardised test MSE of the decoded posterior means over all 111 test fields, against POD with 8 modes (cell 18). I show this curve for context; it played no part in training or in any choice.

def build_vae_dashboard():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7.5))
    ax_r, ax_l, ax_e, ax_m = axes[0, 0], axes[0, 1], axes[1, 0], axes[1, 1]

    ax_r.contour(X_GRID, Y_GRID, sdf_case, levels=[0.0], colors="black", linewidths=1.0)
    fig.colorbar(mesh_r, ax=ax_r, shrink=0.85, label="scaled p")
    ax_r.set_aspect("equal"); ax_r.set_xlabel("x/c"); ax_r.set_ylabel("y/c"); t_r = ax_r.set_title("")
    mesh_e = ax_e.pcolormesh(X_GRID, Y_GRID, all_err[0], shading="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-emax, vmax=emax)
    ax_e.contour(X_GRID, Y_GRID, sdf_case, levels=[0.0], colors="black", linewidths=1.0)
    fig.colorbar(mesh_e, ax=ax_e, shrink=0.85, label="reconstruction − reference")
    ax_e.set_aspect("equal"); ax_e.set_xlabel("x/c"); ax_e.set_ylabel("y/c"); ax_e.set_title("Error of the reconstruction")
    ep_all = np.arange(1, len(final_hist["reconstruction"]) + 1)
    ax_l.set_xlim(0, len(ep_all)); ax_l.set_yscale("log")
    lo = min(min(final_hist["reconstruction"]), min(final_hist["kl"])); hi = max(max(final_hist["reconstruction"]), max(final_hist["kl"]))
    ax_l.set_ylim(lo * 0.5, hi * 2)
    rec_line, = ax_l.plot([], [], lw=2, label="reconstruction")
    kl_line, = ax_l.plot([], [], lw=2, label="KL")
    ax_l.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax_l.set_ylabel("loss term"); ax_l.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.2); ax_l.set_title("Training losses")
    ax_b = ax_l.twinx(); ax_b.set_ylim(0, BETA_MAX * 1.1); ax_b.set_ylabel("β")
    beta_line, = ax_b.plot([], [], "k:", lw=1.5, label="β")
    ax_l.legend(handles=[rec_line, kl_line, beta_line], fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
    ep_s = [s["epoch"] for s in snaps]; mse_s = [s["test_mse"] for s in snaps]
    ax_m.axhline(anim_data["pod_test_mse"], color="tab:gray", ls="--", label="POD, 8 modes")
    mse_line, = ax_m.plot([], [], "o-", ms=3, color="tab:green", label="β-VAE, decoded μ")
    ax_m.set_xlim(0, len(ep_all)); ax_m.set_yscale("log"); ax_m.set_ylim(min(mse_s + [anim_data["pod_test_mse"]]) * 0.7, max(mse_s) * 1.5)
    ax_m.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax_m.set_ylabel("standardised test MSE"); ax_m.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.2)
    ax_m.legend(fontsize=9); ax_m.set_title("Test error over 111 fields (not used for training)")

    def update(k):
        s = snaps[k]; h = s["history"]; e = np.arange(1, len(h["reconstruction"]) + 1)
        mesh_r.set_array(s["recon"][:, :, p_idx].ravel()); mesh_e.set_array(all_err[k].ravel())
        t_r.set_text(f"Reconstructed pressure, test case 0 — epoch {s['epoch']}")
        rec_line.set_data(e, h["reconstruction"]); kl_line.set_data(e, h["kl"])
        beta_line.set_data(e, [BETA_MAX * min(1.0, i / BETA_WARMUP_EPOCHS) for i in e])
        mse_line.set_data(ep_s[:k + 1], mse_s[:k + 1])
        return [mesh_r, mesh_e, rec_line, kl_line, beta_line, mse_line, t_r]

    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, update

Answers — A1 to A3 (numbers from the cell above and the animation of cell 40).

  • A1. The β-VAE's standardised test error over the 111 test fields falls below that of POD with the same 8 coordinates (0.0557) from the snapshot at epoch 56, and ends at 0.0374 after 100 epochs.
  • A2. While β is still small the Kullback–Leibler term first rises (18.9 at epoch 1, 22.0 at epoch 10); by the time β reaches its maximum at epoch 30 it has fallen to 7.2, and it settles at 4.45 by epoch 100. The reconstruction term falls throughout, from 0.990 to 0.0359.
  • A3. The pressure error of the fixed case sits at the surface: its mean absolute error is 0.433 within 0.02 chord, 0.097 between 0.02 and 0.1 chord and 0.032 beyond; the largest error (11.0 in scaled units) is at the leading edge (x/c = 0.004, y/c = 0.008), where the stagnation pressure peaks over a few grid points.

These answers rest on one training run (seed 2026) and one fixed case, and the test-error curve was never used to choose anything.

Task of cell 30 — latent surrogates¶

The task is to pick a target (z_pod_train or z_vae_train), train latent_surrogate with an MSE loss, reconstruct the predicted test fields and separate the reduction error from the surrogate error. I trained both targets.

Where the notebook leaves the settings open, these are my choices. I hold out 15 % of the training rows for early stopping (patience 100, at most 2,000 epochs, batch 32), the same recipe as the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3, because the notebook has no validation set and I did not want to touch the test set while training. I divide each target by one global scale (its standard deviation over all coordinates) rather than scaling each coordinate separately, so that the coordinates keep their relative weight and, for POD, the energy ordering of the modes survives. The main models use SEED; I train two more seeds for the comparisons that depend on the initialisation.

In [24]:
# ================================================================
# Latent surrogates — task of cell 30
# ================================================================
SURR_EPOCHS, SURR_PATIENCE, SURR_BATCH = 2000, 100, 32
SEEDS = [SEED, SEED + 1, SEED + 2]
Z_TRAIN = {"POD": z_pod_train.astype(np.float32), "beta-VAE": z_vae_train}
Z_TEST = {"POD": z_pod_test.astype(np.float32), "beta-VAE": z_vae_test}


def _slug(kind):
    return "pod" if kind == "POD" else "vae"


def train_latent_surrogate(kind, seed):
    folder = MODEL_DIR if seed == SEED else EX_MODEL_DIR
    path = folder / f"latent_surrogate_{_slug(kind)}_seed{seed}.keras"
    meta = path.with_suffix(".json")
    if path.exists() and meta.exists():
        info = json.load(open(meta)); info["net"] = keras.models.load_model(path); return info
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    scale = float(np.std(Z_TRAIN[kind]))
    net = build_latent_surrogate(X_train.shape[1], LATENT_DIM)
    net.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1.0e-3), loss="mse")
    t0 = time.time()
    h = net.fit(X_train, Z_TRAIN[kind] / scale, validation_split=0.15, epochs=SURR_EPOCHS, batch_size=SURR_BATCH,
                shuffle=True, verbose=0,
                callbacks=[EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=SURR_PATIENCE, restore_best_weights=True)])
    info = {"kind": kind, "seed": seed, "scale": scale, "epochs": len(h.history["loss"]),
            "best_epoch": int(np.argmin(h.history["val_loss"])) + 1, "seconds": round(time.time() - t0, 1)}
    net.save(path); json.dump(info, open(meta, "w"))
    info["net"] = net
    return info


def predict_latent(s, X):
    return s["net"].predict(X, verbose=0) * s["scale"]


def decode_pod(z):
    return pod.inverse_transform(np.asarray(z, np.float32)).reshape((-1,) + test_scaled.shape[1:])


def decode_vae(z, dec=None):
    return np.transpose((dec or decoder).predict(np.asarray(z, np.float32), batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0), (0, 3, 1, 2))


DECODE = {"POD": decode_pod, "beta-VAE": decode_vae}

surrogates = {(k, SEED): train_latent_surrogate(k, SEED) for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE")}
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    s = surrogates[(k, SEED)]
    z_hat = predict_latent(s, X_test)
    fields_hat = DECODE[k](z_hat); fields_true_latent = DECODE[k](Z_TEST[k])
    print(f"{k:8s}: epochs {s['epochs']} (best {s['best_epoch']}); reduction MSE "
          f"{np.mean((fields_true_latent - test_scaled) ** 2):.4f}, surrogate MSE "
          f"{np.mean((fields_hat - fields_true_latent) ** 2):.4f}, total MSE {np.mean((fields_hat - test_scaled) ** 2):.4f}")

POD     : epochs 1724 (best 1624); reduction MSE 0.0557, surrogate MSE 0.0011, total MSE 0.0568

beta-VAE: epochs 851 (best 751); reduction MSE 0.0374, surrogate MSE 0.0015, total MSE 0.0381

Task of cell 34 — aerodynamic head¶

The head of cell 34 maps the 8 latent coordinates to $(C_L, C_D)$. I train it on the latent coordinates of the 378 training fields (the POD coordinates, or the β-VAE posterior means) and the coefficients of cell 32. I standardise both inputs and targets with statistics of the training cases only: the drag coefficient is about a hundred times smaller than the lift coefficient, so with unscaled targets lift would dominate the loss. The training settings are those of the latent surrogates.

The complete chain of cell 33 is then: parameters → parameter_scaler → latent surrogate → latent vector → head → $(C_L, C_D)$.

In [25]:
# ================================================================
# Aerodynamic head and the complete chain — task of cell 34
# ================================================================
coef_scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train_coefficients)


def train_head(kind, seed):
    folder = MODEL_DIR if seed == SEED else EX_MODEL_DIR
    path = folder / f"aerodynamic_head_{_slug(kind)}_seed{seed}.keras"
    zpath = path.with_name(path.stem + "_latent_scaler.joblib")
    if path.exists() and zpath.exists():
        return {"net": keras.models.load_model(path), "z_scaler": joblib.load(zpath), "kind": kind, "seed": seed}
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    z_scaler = StandardScaler().fit(Z_TRAIN[kind])
    net = build_aerodynamic_head(LATENT_DIM)
    net.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1.0e-3), loss="mse")
    net.fit(z_scaler.transform(Z_TRAIN[kind]), coef_scaler.transform(train_coefficients), validation_split=0.15,
            epochs=SURR_EPOCHS, batch_size=SURR_BATCH, shuffle=True, verbose=0,
            callbacks=[EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=SURR_PATIENCE, restore_best_weights=True)])
    net.save(path); joblib.dump(z_scaler, zpath)
    return {"net": net, "z_scaler": z_scaler, "kind": kind, "seed": seed}


def predict_head(h, Z):
    return coef_scaler.inverse_transform(h["net"].predict(h["z_scaler"].transform(Z), verbose=0))


def chain_predict(params, kind, seed=SEED):
    """params in the notebook's units: (m, p, t as chord fractions, Re, alpha in degrees)."""
    X = parameter_scaler.transform(prepare_parameters(np.asarray(params, np.float32))).astype(np.float32)
    return predict_head(heads[(kind, seed)], predict_latent(surrogates[(kind, seed)], X))


heads = {(k, SEED): train_head(k, SEED) for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE")}
joblib.dump({"coef_scaler": coef_scaler, "parameter_scaler": parameter_scaler, "parameter_names": PARAMETER_NAMES,
             "parameter_units": "m, p, t as chord fractions; Re absolute (log10 applied before scaling); alpha in degrees",
             "latent_scales": {k: surrogates[(k, SEED)]["scale"] for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE")}},
            MODEL_DIR / "chain_scalers.joblib")

# The coefficient surrogate of Stage 3: inputs (Re/1e6, alpha, m, p, t) with m, p, t as NACA digits
provided_model = keras.models.load_model("../data/airfrans_cl_cd_surrogate.keras")
provided_scalers = joblib.load("../data/airfrans_cl_cd_scalers.joblib")


def provided_predict(params):
    P_ = np.asarray(params, dtype=np.float64)
    x = np.column_stack([P_[:, 3] / 1.0e6, P_[:, 4], P_[:, 0] * 100.0, P_[:, 1] * 10.0, P_[:, 2] * 100.0])
    return provided_scalers["y_scaler"].inverse_transform(
        provided_model.predict(provided_scalers["x_scaler"].transform(x), verbose=0))


check = provided_predict(test_parameters)
print("Unit check, provided surrogate on the 111 test cases: CL RMSE "
      f"{np.sqrt(np.mean((check[:, 0] - test_coefficients[:, 0]) ** 2)):.6f}, CD RMSE "
      f"{np.sqrt(np.mean((check[:, 1] - test_coefficients[:, 1]) ** 2)):.6f}")
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    pred = chain_predict(test_parameters, k)
    print(f"Chain via {k:8s}: CL RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((pred[:, 0] - test_coefficients[:, 0]) ** 2)):.4f}, "
          f"CD RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((pred[:, 1] - test_coefficients[:, 1]) ** 2)):.5f}")

Chain via beta-VAE: CL RMSE 0.0238, CD RMSE 0.00074

Part C — Project questions¶

I take the eight questions of cell 35 in order; each gets its code, its output and an answer cell. Unless a question changes them, the data split, the scaling and the settings are those of Parts A and B. Wherever a comparison depends on a random initialisation I repeat it with three seeds (SEED, SEED + 1, SEED + 2) and report mean ± standard deviation; errors of fields are mean squared errors in the standardised units of cell 16 ("standardised MSE"), and every table and figure goes to results/. Questions 1–4 locate where the error comes from, question 5 decides whether the chain is good enough to screen designs, and questions 6–8 test how far the design search can be trusted.

Question 1 — POD modes for 95 % and 99 % of the variance; a latent-size sweep¶

This cell fits a full POD (PCA with all 378 components) on the training snapshots only and reads the number of modes for 95 % and 99 % of the cumulative explained variance. For 8, 10, 20 and 30 modes it also reports the variance captured and the standardised test MSE.

In [26]:
pca_full = PCA(svd_solver="full").fit(train_snapshots)
cum = np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_)
n95, n99 = int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.95) + 1), int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.99) + 1)
z_full_test = pca_full.transform(test_snapshots)
rows = []
for k in (8, 10, 20, 30, n95, n99):
    rec = (z_full_test[:, :k] @ pca_full.components_[:k] + pca_full.mean_).reshape(test_scaled.shape)
    per_ch = ((rec - test_scaled) ** 2).mean(axis=(0, 2, 3))
    rows.append({"modes": k, "variance_captured_train": float(cum[k - 1]), "test_mse": float(np.mean((rec - test_scaled) ** 2)),
                 **{f"test_mse_{c}": float(v) for c, v in zip(channel_names, per_ch)}})
ex1_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).drop_duplicates("modes").sort_values("modes")
ex1_table.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex1_pod_modes.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame({"modes": np.arange(1, len(cum) + 1), "cumulative_variance": cum}).to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex1_pod_cumulative_variance.csv", index=False)
print(f"Modes for 95% of the training variance: {n95}; for 99%: {n99} (of {len(cum)})")
print(f"Cell 18 (randomised solver, 8 modes): variance {pod.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.4f}, test MSE {pod_test_mse:.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

Question 2 — POD or β-VAE at the same latent dimension?¶

Both use 8 coordinates, and this cell reports the error per channel. Because the β-VAE depends on its initialisation, I train it with three seeds: the run of cell 24 (SEED) and two more runs with SEED + 1 and SEED + 2, each a copy of the cell 24 loop with only the seed changed. POD has no random element.

In [27]:
def train_beta_vae(seed):
    enc_path, dec_path = EX_MODEL_DIR / f"beta_vae_seed{seed}_encoder.keras", EX_MODEL_DIR / f"beta_vae_seed{seed}_decoder.keras"
    if enc_path.exists() and dec_path.exists():
        return (keras.models.load_model(enc_path, custom_objects={"Sampling": Sampling}), keras.models.load_model(dec_path))
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    ds = (tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(train_images).shuffle(len(train_images), seed=seed, reshuffle_each_iteration=True)
          .batch(BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE))
    enc, dec = build_beta_vae(input_shape=train_images.shape[1:], latent_dim=LATENT_DIM)
    opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)
    for epoch in range(N_EPOCHS):
        b = BETA_MAX * min(1.0, (epoch + 1) / BETA_WARMUP_EPOCHS)
        for batch in ds:
            with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
                mu_b, logvar_b, z_b = enc(batch, training=True)
                total, _, _ = beta_vae_loss(dec(z_b, training=True), batch, mu_b, logvar_b, b)
            variables = enc.trainable_variables + dec.trainable_variables
            opt.apply_gradients(zip(tape.gradient(total, variables), variables))
    enc.save(enc_path); dec.save(dec_path)
    return enc, dec


vae_models = {SEED: (encoder, decoder)}
for s in SEEDS[1:]:
    loaded = (EX_MODEL_DIR / f"beta_vae_seed{s}_encoder.keras").exists()
    t0 = time.time(); vae_models[s] = train_beta_vae(s)
    print(f"beta-VAE seed {s}: {'loaded from the saved exercise models' if loaded else f'trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s'}")

Answer — Q2. The β-VAE reconstructs unseen fields better at the same latent dimension. With 8 coordinates its standardised test error is 0.0375 ± 0.0022 over three seeds (0.0374, 0.0353, 0.0397) against 0.0557 for POD, a gap about eight times the seed spread. The gain is in the streamwise velocity (0.0466 against 0.0725), the pressure (0.0312 against 0.0374) and above all the turbulent-viscosity channel (0.0901 against 0.1565); POD stays better for the vertical velocity (0.0108 against 0.0148) and the signed distance (0.0016 against 0.0046). Three training runs are enough to separate the two models here, but not to pin the β-VAE's error more finely than its spread.

Question 3 — Which variables and regions are hardest to reconstruct?¶

For POD and the β-VAE (seed 2026) this cell averages the squared error over the 111 test fields at every grid point, per channel, and draws it with the outline of the mean test signed-distance field (the airfoils differ, so this outline is an average shape). It also averages the error by distance band from each case's own surface: inside the body, within 0.02 chord, 0.02–0.1 chord, beyond 0.1 chord.

Question 4 — Reduction error against latent-surrogate error¶

For each reduced model I separate three errors: the reduction error decodes the true latent coordinates of the test fields; the surrogate error compares the field decoded from the predicted coordinates with the field decoded from the true ones; the total error compares the field decoded from the predicted coordinates with the reference. As latent predictors I use the MLP of cell 30 (three seeds), a linear fit from the scaled parameters, and the mean of the training coordinates (a predictor that ignores the parameters).

In [29]:
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    for s in SEEDS[1:]:
        surrogates[(k, s)] = train_latent_surrogate(k, s)

rows = []
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    true_dec = DECODE[k](Z_TEST[k])
    reduction = float(np.mean((true_dec - test_scaled) ** 2))
    predictors = {f"MLP seed {s}": predict_latent(surrogates[(k, s)], X_test) for s in SEEDS}
    predictors["linear fit"] = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, Z_TRAIN[k]).predict(X_test)
    predictors["training mean"] = np.repeat(Z_TRAIN[k].mean(axis=0, keepdims=True), len(X_test), axis=0)
    for name, z_hat in predictors.items():
        dec_hat = DECODE[k](z_hat)
        rows.append({"reduced_model": k, "latent_predictor": name, "reduction_mse": reduction,
                     "surrogate_mse": float(np.mean((dec_hat - true_dec) ** 2)),

With the MLP latent surrogate (three seeds) POD gives 0.0557 reduction + 0.0014 ± 0.0003 surrogate = 0.0571 total, and the β-VAE 0.0374 + 0.0013 ± 0.0002 = 0.0380, so the surrogate adds 2–4 % to the field error. For the pressure channel alone the totals are 0.0384 (POD) and 0.0314 (β-VAE). What this does not show is the seed-to-seed spread of the reduction itself, since the reduction error is that of one β-VAE (seed 2026) while the MLP error is averaged over three.

Question 5 — Can the latent representation predict $C_L$ and $C_D$ for design screening?¶

This cell scores the following on the 111 test cases with MAE, RMSE and $R^2$ per coefficient:

  • the complete chain parameters → latent surrogate → predicted latent → head, for POD and the β-VAE (three seeds of surrogate and head);
  • the same chain with a linear regression from the latent coordinates in place of the head;
  • the head applied to the true latent coordinates of the test fields, a diagnostic only, since it needs the simulated field;
  • the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3, queried directly with the same 111 cases (it was trained on the same 378 training cases);
  • the mean of the training coefficients, as the simplest reference.
In [30]:
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    for s in SEEDS[1:]:
        heads[(k, s)] = train_head(k, s)


def scores(pred, label, **extra):
    out = {"model": label, **extra}
    for j, c in enumerate(["CL", "CD"]):
        y = test_coefficients[:, j]
        out[f"{c}_MAE"] = float(mean_absolute_error(y, pred[:, j]))
        out[f"{c}_RMSE"] = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((pred[:, j] - y) ** 2)))
        out[f"{c}_R2"] = float(r2_score(y, pred[:, j]))
    return out


rows = [scores(np.repeat(train_coefficients.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True), len(test_parameters), axis=0), "training mean"),
        scores(provided_predict(test_parameters), "coefficient surrogate of Stage 3")]
for k in ("POD", "beta-VAE"):
    lin_head = LinearRegression().fit(Z_TRAIN[k], train_coefficients)
    for s in SEEDS:
        z_hat = predict_latent(surrogates[(k, s)], X_test)
        rows.append(scores(predict_head(heads[(k, s)], z_hat), f"chain via {k}, MLP head", seed=s))
        rows.append(scores(lin_head.predict(z_hat), f"chain via {k}, linear head", seed=s))
        rows.append(scores(predict_head(heads[(k, s)], Z_TEST[k]), f"MLP head on true {k} latents (diagnostic)", seed=s))
    rows.append(scores(lin_head.predict(Z_TEST[k]), f"linear head on true {k} latents (diagnostic)"))
ex5_runs = pd.DataFrame(rows); ex5_runs.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex5_aerodynamic_head_runs.csv", index=False)
metrics = [c for c in ex5_runs.columns if c.endswith(("MAE", "RMSE", "R2"))]
g = ex5_runs.groupby("model", sort=False)
ex5_summary = g[metrics].mean().join(g[["CL_RMSE", "CD_RMSE", "CL_R2", "CD_R2"]].std().add_suffix("_std")).join(g.size().rename("runs")).reset_index()
ex5_summary.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex5_aerodynamic_head_summary.csv", index=False)
ex5_summary.round(5)

Answer — Q5. Yes, the chain is accurate enough to screen designs. On the 111 test cases the complete β-VAE chain (parameters → latent surrogate → head) reaches $C_L$ RMSE 0.0212 ± 0.0023 ($R^2$ 0.9986) and $C_D$ RMSE 0.00074 ± 0.00002 ($R^2$ 0.980) over three seeds, slightly better than the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3 queried on the same cases (0.0259 and 0.00087; $R^2$ 0.9979 and 0.972) and better than the POD chain (0.0275 and 0.00104). Predicting the training mean gives 0.571 and 0.0052. A linear head is clearly worse for the β-VAE (0.0450 and 0.00176), so the nonlinearity of the head matters; the head on the true latent coordinates (0.0177 and 0.00057) shows what the latent surrogate costs. Two things to keep in mind: the Stage 3 surrogate is one model against the mean of three seeds, and all the test cases lie inside the training ranges.

Question 6 — Which admissible design maximises $C_L/C_D$?¶

I chose $Re = 4\times10^6$ and $\alpha = 5^\circ$, the operating point of the flap-control stages (Stages 2 and 4), and built a grid of four-digit candidates inside the training ranges of $m$, $p$ and $t$ (15 × 15 × 16 = 3,600 candidates, each range read from the training parameters). This cell predicts $C_L/C_D$ with the β-VAE chain, the POD chain (seed 2026) and the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3, reports each model's best design with its value under the other models, and searches the other two seeds of each chain to see whether the choice is stable. Following cell 33, it also decodes the predicted pressure field of the chosen design.

In [31]:
RE_DESIGN, ALPHA_DESIGN = 4.0e6, 5.0
lo_p, hi_p = train_parameters.min(axis=0), train_parameters.max(axis=0)
grid_m, grid_p, grid_t = np.linspace(lo_p[0], hi_p[0], 15), np.linspace(lo_p[1], hi_p[1], 15), np.linspace(lo_p[2], hi_p[2], 16)
M_, P_, T_ = np.meshgrid(grid_m, grid_p, grid_t, indexing="ij")
candidates = np.column_stack([M_.ravel(), P_.ravel(), T_.ravel(), np.full(M_.size, RE_DESIGN), np.full(M_.size, ALPHA_DESIGN)]).astype(np.float32)
print("Candidates:", candidates.shape, "| ranges m", lo_p[0], hi_p[0], "p", lo_p[1], hi_p[1], "t", lo_p[2], hi_p[2])

predictions = {"beta-VAE chain": chain_predict(candidates, "beta-VAE"), "POD chain": chain_predict(candidates, "POD"),
               "coefficient surrogate (Stage 3)": provided_predict(candidates)}
rows, best = [], {}
for name, pred in predictions.items():
    ratio = pred[:, 0] / pred[:, 1]; i = int(np.argmax(ratio)); best[name] = i
    row = {"selected_by": name, "m_digit": candidates[i, 0] * 100, "p_digit": candidates[i, 1] * 10, "t_digit": candidates[i, 2] * 100,
           "on_edge_of_box": bool(np.any(np.isclose(candidates[i, :3], lo_p[:3]) | np.isclose(candidates[i, :3], hi_p[:3])))}
    for other, op in predictions.items():
        row[f"CL/CD by {other}"] = float(op[i, 0] / op[i, 1]); row[f"CL by {other}"] = float(op[i, 0])
    rows.append(row)
for k in ("beta-VAE", "POD"):
    for s in SEEDS[1:]:
        pred = chain_predict(candidates, k, s); i = int(np.argmax(pred[:, 0] / pred[:, 1]))
        rows.append({"selected_by": f"{k} chain, seed {s}", "m_digit": candidates[i, 0] * 100, "p_digit": candidates[i, 1] * 10,
                     "t_digit": candidates[i, 2] * 100, f"CL/CD by {k} chain": float(pred[i, 0] / pred[i, 1])})
ex6_table = pd.DataFrame(rows); ex6_table.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex6_design_search.csv", index=False)
same = best["beta-VAE chain"] == best["coefficient surrogate (Stage 3)"]
print("beta-VAE chain and coefficient surrogate (Stage 3) pick the same candidate:", same)

i_vae = best["beta-VAE chain"]
X_best = parameter_scaler.transform(prepare_parameters(candidates[i_vae:i_vae + 1])).astype(np.float32)
field_best = decode_vae(predict_latent(surrogates[("beta-VAE", SEED)], X_best))[0] * channel_std[0] + channel_mean[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))

Answer — Q6. The three models agree on a thin, strongly cambered section with the camber in the front half, but not on which one. The β-VAE chain picks m 6.0, p 5.0, t 5.09 (predicted $C_L/C_D$ 125.3 by itself, 103.0 by the POD chain, 113.0 by the Stage 3 surrogate); the POD chain m 6.5, p 4.5, t 5.09 (121.0 / 104.9 / 115.1); the Stage 3 surrogate m 7.0, p 3.5, t 5.09 (106.2 / 103.2 / 116.5). The other seeds of the β-VAE chain pick m 5.0, p 5.0 (117.7) and m 7.0, p 3.0 (126.5), and those of the POD chain m 6.0 and 6.5 with p 3.5. I would not trust any single pick: every one lies on the thin edge of the training box (t = 5.09 % is the smallest thickness in the data), the pick changes with the seed, and no simulation confirms any of them.

Question 8 — Is the optimum close to the training data?¶

I measure distances in the space the latent surrogate sees: the five parameters after prepare_parameters and parameter_scaler (standardised, $\log_{10} Re$). For each selected design the distance to the nearest training case is compared with the same distance for the 111 test cases, which the models handle well (questions 4 and 5). I also give distances on the three shape parameters alone, because the operating point ($Re$, $\alpha$) is fixed by the search.

In [33]:
S_train = parameter_scaler.transform(prepare_parameters(train_parameters))
S_test = parameter_scaler.transform(prepare_parameters(test_parameters))
def nearest(S, idx=slice(None)):
    d = np.sqrt(((S[:, None, idx] - S_train[None, :, idx]) ** 2).sum(axis=-1)); return d.min(axis=1), d.argmin(axis=1)
test_d5, _ = nearest(S_test); test_d3, _ = nearest(S_test, slice(0, 3))
rows = []
for dname, d in designs.items():

             "nearest_training_case": f"median; 95th percentile 5d {np.percentile(test_d5, 95):.3f}, shape {np.percentile(test_d3, 95):.3f}; max 5d {test_d5.max():.3f}"})

Answer — Q8. In the five standardised inputs the surrogate sees, both optima are as close to a training case as a typical test case: distance 0.730 (β-VAE chain's design) and 0.805 (Stage 3 surrogate's design) against a median of 0.759 and a 95th percentile of 1.134 over the 111 test cases (42nd and 60th percentile). In shape alone the picture differs: the β-VAE chain's design is at 0.285 (54th percentile), while the Stage 3 surrogate's design is at 0.530, farther from any training shape than 96 % of the test cases. The nearest training case of both is a section with m 6.7, p 4.6, t 6.1 at 6.8°. Since both designs sit on the thinnest edge of the data (t = 5.09 %), the search interpolates along the edge of the box rather than inside it.

Part D — Four additions¶

Four additions that go beyond the eight questions. In D1 I use the three seeds of the β-VAE chain as an ensemble and ask where in the design space the chains disagree and whether their spread tracks the error on unseen cases. In D2 I open the β-VAE's latent space: which coordinates are active, what each one correlates with, and where in the field each one acts. In D3 I measure what a query costs on this machine, and in D4 I map the project onto an eight-step modelling workflow. Each block ends with an answer cell.

D1 — Ensemble uncertainty over the design space¶

Questions 5 and 6 showed that the three seeds of the β-VAE chain score the test cases alike but pick different cambers as the optimum. Here I use the three chains together as an ensemble. Which three chains: for seed $s$ the chain is the latent surrogate and the aerodynamic head initialised with seed $s$ (seed 2026 in trained_models/, 2027 and 2028 in trained_models/exercises/), each with its own latent scaler; the parameter scaler of cell 29 and the coefficient scaler of cell 48 are shared. All three surrogates and heads were trained on the latent coordinates of the β-VAE of cell 24 (seed 2026; see Z_TRAIN in cell 46), so the ensemble spread measures the initialisation of the surrogate and the head, not that of the β-VAE; the two extra β-VAEs of question 2 are not part of the chains.

This cell scores the full question-6 grid ($Re = 4\times10^6$, $\alpha = 5^\circ$, 15 × 15 × 16 = 3,600 candidates) with the three chains and computes, per candidate, the mean and the standard deviation (over the three seeds, sample standard deviation) of $C_L$, $C_D$ and $C_L/C_D$. It reports the spread at the three question-6 picks against the median spread over the grid; maps of the $C_L/C_D$ mean and spread over $(m, p)$ at $t = 5.09\,\%$ (the thinnest grid value, where all picks lie) and at $t \approx 12\,\%$; and a calibration check on the 111 test cases: the ensemble standard deviation of $C_L$ against the absolute error of the ensemble mean (scatter, Spearman rank correlation, and the mean error of the 20 % of cases with the largest spread against the other 80 %).

Answer — D1. The spread is largest exactly where the optima sit. Over the 3,600 candidates the median spread of the three chains is 0.0141 in $C_L$, 0.00032 in $C_D$ and 2.58 in $C_L/C_D$; at the three question-6 picks the $C_L/C_D$ spread is 6.95 (β-VAE chain's pick, 2.7 × the median, 95th percentile of the grid), 6.75 (POD chain's pick, 2.6 ×, 94th) and 11.69 (Stage 3 surrogate's pick, 4.5 ×, above 99.9 % of the grid). The maps show why: the chains disagree most in the thin, highly cambered corner where all the optima lie, and the median spread falls from 4.55 at t = 5.1 % to 2.04 at t = 19.9 %. The candidate with the highest ensemble-mean $C_L/C_D$ (m 5.5, p 5.0, t 5.09; 118.1 ± 5.6) has 46 other candidates within one spread of it, so the ensemble cannot rank the top of the grid.

On unseen cases the spread tracks the error, but only weakly. For the 111 test cases the ensemble standard deviation of $C_L$ and the absolute error of the ensemble mean have a Spearman rank correlation of 0.29 (p = 0.002); the 22 cases with the largest spread have a mean error of 0.0158 against 0.0107 for the other 89 (1.5 ×). For $C_D$ the correlation is 0.16 (p = 0.10) and the ratio 2.0. The spread is therefore a useful flag rather than a calibrated error bar: the scatter shows errors of 0.03–0.04 at spreads below 0.01. Averaging the three chains also lowers the test RMSE from 0.0212 (mean single seed) to 0.0152 for $C_L$ and from 0.00074 to 0.00063 for $C_D$. With three members that share one β-VAE, the spread measures the initialisation of the surrogate and the head only, which is a lower bound on the real disagreement one could expect.

D2 — What the latent coordinates encode¶

With the β-VAE of cell 24 (seed 2026) this cell encodes the 378 training fields to their posterior means $\mu$, the same coordinates the surrogate of cell 46 predicts, and reads the latent space in three ways:

  • Activity. The standard deviation of each $\mu_k$ across the training fields, compared with the mean posterior standard deviation $\exp(\tfrac12 \log\sigma^2_k)$ of that coordinate. A coordinate whose $\mu_k$ barely moves between fields, while its posterior noise is of order one, carries no information (the Kullback–Leibler term has pushed it back to the prior); I call it inactive. The per-coordinate Kullback–Leibler term is listed as a second measure.
  • Correlations. The 8 × 8 correlation matrix of $\mu$ (whether the coordinates are redundant) and the 8 × 5 correlation of $\mu$ with the parameters $(m, p, t, \log_{10} Re, \alpha)$ (what each coordinate follows).
  • Traversal. I decode the mean latent vector with coordinate $k$ moved to its mean ± 2 standard deviations, $k = 1 … 8$; the panel shows the difference of the two decoded pressure fields, decode(+2σ) − decode(−2σ), in units of $p / U_\infty^2$, with the outline of the mean decoded shape (zero level of the decoded signed distance) drawn on each panel. The colour scale is shared, so an inactive coordinate would show an empty panel.
In [35]:
# ================================================================
# D2 — What the latent coordinates encode
# ================================================================
mu_tr, logvar_tr, _ = encoder.predict(train_images, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, verbose=0)    # notebook beta-VAE, 378 training fields
mu_std = mu_tr.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
post_sigma = np.exp(0.5 * logvar_tr).mean(axis=0)
kl_per_coord = (-0.5 * (1.0 + logvar_tr - mu_tr ** 2 - np.exp(logvar_tr))).mean(axis=0)
active = mu_std > post_sigma
P_tr = prepare_parameters(train_parameters)                                               # m, p, t, log10 Re, alpha
param_labels = ["m", "p", "t", "log10 Re", "alpha"]
corr_mu = np.corrcoef(mu_tr, rowvar=False)
corr_mp = np.corrcoef(np.hstack([mu_tr, P_tr]), rowvar=False)[:LATENT_DIM, LATENT_DIM:]
ex10_stats = pd.DataFrame({"coordinate": np.arange(1, LATENT_DIM + 1), "mu_mean": mu_tr.mean(axis=0), "mu_std": mu_std,
                           "posterior_sigma_mean": post_sigma, "kl_per_coordinate": kl_per_coord, "active": active,
                           "most_correlated_parameter": [param_labels[j] for j in np.argmax(np.abs(corr_mp), axis=1)],
                           "correlation_with_it": corr_mp[np.arange(LATENT_DIM), np.argmax(np.abs(corr_mp), axis=1)],
                           **{f"corr_{l}": corr_mp[:, j] for j, l in enumerate(param_labels)}})
print(f"Active coordinates (std of mu across fields > mean posterior sigma): {int(active.sum())} of {LATENT_DIM}")
print("Largest |correlation| between two different coordinates:", f"{np.abs(corr_mu - np.eye(LATENT_DIM)).max():.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [8, 5.4]})
for ax, mat, xl, title in ((axes[0], corr_mu, [f"μ{k}" for k in range(1, 9)], "Correlation between latent coordinates (378 training fields)"),
                           (axes[1], corr_mp, param_labels, "Correlation of latent coordinates with the parameters")):
    im = ax.imshow(mat, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(mat.shape[1])); ax.set_xticklabels(xl); ax.set_yticks(range(LATENT_DIM)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"μ{k}" for k in range(1, 9)])
    for (r, c), v in np.ndenumerate(mat):
        ax.text(c, r, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color="white" if abs(v) > 0.6 else "black")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10); fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="Pearson correlation")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(RES_DIR / "ex10_latent_correlations.png", dpi=120); plt.show()

# --- traversal: mean latent vector with coordinate k at mean ± 2 std ---
mu_bar = mu_tr.mean(axis=0)
Z_trav = np.repeat(mu_bar[None, :], 2 * LATENT_DIM, axis=0)
for k in range(LATENT_DIM):
    Z_trav[2 * k, k] += 2 * mu_std[k]; Z_trav[2 * k + 1, k] -= 2 * mu_std[k]
dec_trav = decode_vae(Z_trav) * channel_std[0] + channel_mean[0]                            # physical units, channels first
base_field = decode_vae(mu_bar[None, :])[0] * channel_std[0] + channel_mean[0]
p_idx = channel_names.index("p_over_Uinf2")
diff_p = dec_trav[0::2, p_idx] - dec_trav[1::2, p_idx]                                     # (8, NY, NX): decode(+2σ) − decode(−2σ)
near = base_field[sdf_index] < 0.1                                                          # within 0.1 chord of the decoded mean shape (or inside it)
trav_rows = []
for k in range(LATENT_DIM):
    a = np.abs(diff_p[k]); iy, ix = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(a), a.shape)
    trav_rows.append({"coordinate": k + 1, "max_abs_dp": float(a.max()), "x_c_of_max": float(x_grid[ix]), "y_c_of_max": float(y_grid[iy]),
                      "side_of_max": "upper (y > 0)" if y_grid[iy] > 0 else "lower (y <= 0)",
                      "share_of_abs_dp_within_0.1c": float(a[near].sum() / a.sum()),
                      "mean_dp_upper_near": float(diff_p[k][near & (Y_GRID > 0)].mean()), "mean_dp_lower_near": float(diff_p[k][near & (Y_GRID <= 0)].mean())})
ex10_trav = pd.DataFrame(trav_rows)
ex10_stats = ex10_stats.merge(ex10_trav, on="coordinate")
ex10_stats.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex10_latent_statistics.csv", index=False)

vlim = float(np.percentile(np.abs(diff_p), 99.5))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(20, 6.4), constrained_layout=True)
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.ravel()):
    im = ax.pcolormesh(X_GRID, Y_GRID, diff_p[k], shading="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vlim, vmax=vlim)
    ax.contour(X_GRID, Y_GRID, base_field[sdf_index], levels=[0.0], colors="black", linewidths=1.0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x/c"); ax.set_ylabel("y/c")
    ax.set_title(f"μ{k + 1}: std {mu_std[k]:.2f}, {'active' if active[k] else 'inactive'}, ~{ex10_stats.most_correlated_parameter[k]} "
                 f"(r = {ex10_stats.correlation_with_it[k]:+.2f}); max |Δp| {trav_rows[k]['max_abs_dp']:.3f}", fontsize=9)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes.ravel().tolist(), shrink=0.8, label="Δ p/U∞²: decode(mean + 2σ) − decode(mean − 2σ)")
fig.suptitle("Latent traversal of the beta-VAE (seed 2026): pressure difference per coordinate; black: outline of the decoded mean shape")
fig.savefig(RES_DIR / "ex10_latent_traversal.png", dpi=110); plt.show()
ex10_stats.round(3)

Answer — D2. All eight coordinates are active, and each follows one or two of the shape and flow parameters. The standard deviation of $\mu_k$ across the training fields is 1.30–2.34 while the posterior standard deviation is 0.055–0.080, and the Kullback–Leibler term per coordinate is 3.9–5.1. The coordinates are not independent (largest correlation between two coordinates 0.64, between $\mu_4$ and $\mu_8$; also ±0.53 for $\mu_1$–$\mu_8$, $\mu_2$–$\mu_3$ and $\mu_2$–$\mu_5$, and −0.54 for $\mu_6$–$\mu_7$).

Parameter each coordinate follows most (Pearson correlation) and what its traversal shows (difference of the decoded pressure between +2σ and −2σ, largest change given in $p/U_\infty^2$):

Coordinate Follows Traversal panel
$\mu_1$ α (−0.35) a thin band of higher pressure along the upper surface, largest at the leading edge (0.74)
$\mu_2$ t (+0.74) higher pressure above and lower below over a broad region around the body (0.82 at the leading edge): a thickness-like, symmetric change
$\mu_3$ p (+0.39) the weakest coordinate (0.32), acting at the nose on the lower side
$\mu_4$ m (+0.38) higher pressure in a band along the upper surface (0.71), with a small opposite change at the nose
$\mu_5$ t (+0.80) a thin band along the upper surface near the nose (0.34), little elsewhere
$\mu_6$ α (+0.90) the strongest coordinate (1.82): suction over the whole upper side and higher pressure below, the pattern of a change in angle of attack or circulation, reaching far into the field
$\mu_7$ α (−0.79) the same pattern with the opposite sign (0.99)
$\mu_8$ m (+0.47), with p (+0.45) and t (+0.42) lower pressure above the rear half of the upper surface and higher pressure at the nose (0.54)

No coordinate follows $\log_{10} Re$ (|correlation| ≤ 0.06): the Reynolds number leaves no linear trace in the latent space. The change of each coordinate is spread over the field, not confined to the near field: 14–25 % of the absolute pressure change lies within 0.1 chord of the decoded mean shape, a region that holds about 15 % of the grid points. The largest change of every coordinate is on the upper side, six of eight at the leading edge. I read these panels as tendencies, not as independent effects: the correlations are linear, the traversal is one straight line through the mean latent vector, and the coordinates are coupled.

D3 — Cost of a query¶

What the chain costs on this machine, measured and nothing else: this cell times chain_predict on the 3,600 candidates of question 6 (parameters → latent surrogate → head → $C_L$, $C_D$) and the decoding of one field from a latent vector, three times each after one warm-up call, and for comparison the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3 on the same 3,600 candidates. The training times of the latent surrogates are those recorded when they were trained (the .json files next to the models in trained_models/, written by cell 46). I assume no solver time and quote none: the simulations behind the data were not run here, so I can say what a surrogate query costs but not what it saves.

# D3 — Cost of a query on this machine
# ================================================================
import platform, subprocess
cpu_name = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip() or platform.processor()
print(f"Machine: {cpu_name}, {platform.machine()}, {platform.system()} {platform.release()}; TensorFlow {tf.__version__}; "
      f"GPU available: {len(gpus) > 0}")


def timed(fn, repeats=3):
    fn()                                                       # warm-up: Keras builds its predict function on the first call
    out = []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); out.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return out


X_one = parameter_scaler.transform(prepare_parameters(candidates[best["beta-VAE chain"]:best["beta-VAE chain"] + 1])).astype(np.float32)
measurements = [
    ("beta-VAE chain, 3,600 candidates → (CL, CD)", 3600, lambda: chain_predict(candidates, "beta-VAE")),
    ("beta-VAE chain, 1 candidate → (CL, CD)", 1, lambda: chain_predict(candidates[:1], "beta-VAE")),
    ("decoder, 1 latent vector → full field (5 × 64 × 128)", 1, lambda: decode_vae(mu_bar[None, :])),
    ("surrogate + decoder, 1 design → full field", 1, lambda: decode_vae(predict_latent(surrogates[("beta-VAE", SEED)], X_one))),
    ("coefficient surrogate (Stage 3), 3,600 candidates", 3600, lambda: provided_predict(candidates)),
]
rows = []
for label, n, fn in measurements:
    t = timed(fn)
    rows.append({"item": label, "kind": "measured now (3 repeats after warm-up)", "n_queries": n, "seconds_mean": np.mean(t),
                 "seconds_min": np.min(t), "seconds_max": np.max(t), "ms_per_query": 1000 * np.mean(t) / n})
for (k, s), info in sorted(surrogates.items(), key=lambda kv: (kv[0][0], kv[0][1])):
    rows.append({"item": f"training of the {k} latent surrogate, seed {s} ({info['epochs']} epochs, early stopping)",
                 "kind": "recorded when trained (.json next to the model)", "n_queries": np.nan, "seconds_mean": info["seconds"],
                 "seconds_min": np.nan, "seconds_max": np.nan, "ms_per_query": np.nan})
ex11 = pd.DataFrame(rows); ex11.to_csv(RES_DIR / "ex11_query_cost.csv", index=False)
print("Not measured here: the training time of the beta-VAE and of the aerodynamic heads (not recorded by their cells), "
      "and any solver time (no simulation was run).")
ex11.round(4)

Answer — D3. A query of the chain costs a fraction of a millisecond per design once the batch is large, and tens of milliseconds for a single design or a single field. Measured on an Apple M3 Max, CPU only, TensorFlow 2.21, three repeats after a warm-up call: the β-VAE chain scores the 3,600 candidates of question 6 in 0.106 s (0.105–0.108 s), 0.029 ms per candidate; a single candidate takes 40.0 ms, which is the fixed cost of the two Keras predictions, not the arithmetic; decoding one latent vector to the full 5 × 64 × 128 field takes 19.7 ms, and one design to its field 38.8 ms. The Stage 3 coefficient surrogate scores the same 3,600 candidates in 0.046 s. The recorded training times of the latent surrogates were 38.1, 31.7 and 23.7 s for the POD targets and 18.7, 19.2 and 29.2 s for the β-VAE targets (early stopping, 851–1,724 epochs); training the β-VAE for 100 epochs took 73 s in this environment. Left unmeasured are the training time of the aerodynamic heads, which their cells do not record, and any solver time: no simulation was run, so I can say what a query costs but not what it saves.

D4 — How this project follows an eight-step modelling workflow¶

Step What it means here Cells Baseline used at that step
1. Load Read the two .npz files (378 training and 111 test simulations, 5 channels on a 64 × 128 grid, 5 parameters) and the coefficient table 5–8, 32 —
2. Shape Inspect one simulation and its five channels; keep the channels-first tensor for POD and a channels-last copy for the convolutional β-VAE 10–14, 24 —
3. Split The split comes with the data: training and test files whose case names match the coefficient table one to one; 15 % of the training rows are held out for early stopping of the surrogates and heads 7, 46, 48 —
4. Normalise Each channel standardised with training statistics only; parameters standardised after $\log_{10} Re$; latent targets divided by one global scale; head inputs and targets standardised 16, 29, 46, 48 —
5. Baseline POD with 8 modes as the linear reduced model; the training mean and a linear fit as latent predictors; a linear head; the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3 18, 51, 60, 63 POD against the β-VAE; training mean and linear fit against the latent surrogate; linear head and the Stage 3 coefficient surrogate against the aerodynamic head
6. Model The β-VAE (8 coordinates, β warm-up), the latent surrogate (parameters → μ), the aerodynamic head (μ → $C_L$, $C_D$), chained 23–24, 46, 48 POD (reduction); training mean and linear fit (surrogate); linear head and the Stage 3 surrogate (head)
7. Evaluate Standardised test MSE per channel and per region; reduction against surrogate error; MAE, RMSE and $R^2$ of $C_L$ and $C_D$ on the 111 test cases, three seeds; ensemble calibration 25, 51–63, D1 POD against the β-VAE; training mean and linear fit against the latent surrogate; linear head and the Stage 3 surrogate against the head
8. Interpret The design search and its polar, distance of the optimum to the training data, ensemble spread over the design space, what the latent coordinates encode, the cost of a query 66–72, D1–D3 The three models' picks compared with one another; the test cases as the reference distance

Part E — Summary¶

The table below collects my answers of Parts B–D in one place, and the last cell lists every file the notebook saved (results/, trained_models/, animations/).

Summary of the answers (Parts B–D)¶

One line per question and per added section, with the numbers of the cells above.

# Finding
1 33 POD modes hold 95 % of the training variance and 128 hold 99 % (of 378). Test MSE (standardised): 0.0557 with 8 modes, 0.0498 with 10, 0.0334 with 20, 0.0265 with 30.
2 At 8 coordinates the β-VAE reconstructs unseen fields better overall: 0.0375 ± 0.0022 (3 seeds) against 0.0557 for POD. It is better for u, p and the turbulent-viscosity channel, worse for v (0.0148 against 0.0108) and the signed distance (0.0046 against 0.0016).
3 The turbulent-viscosity channel is the hardest (0.156 POD, 0.090 β-VAE), then u. Within 0.02 chord of the surface the error is two to three orders of magnitude larger than beyond 0.1 chord (turbulent viscosity: 4.69 against 0.052 for POD, 3.08 against 0.015 for the β-VAE).
4 The reduction dominates: POD 0.0557 reduction + 0.0014 surrogate → 0.0571 total; β-VAE 0.0374 + 0.0013 → 0.0380 (3 seeds). A linear fit of the latent coordinates adds 0.060 (POD) and 0.056 (β-VAE); predicting the training mean adds 0.33 and 0.39.
5 The β-VAE chain predicts the coefficients about as well as the coefficient surrogate of Stage 3, on the same 111 cases: $C_L$ RMSE 0.0212 ± 0.0023 against 0.0259, $C_D$ RMSE 0.00074 against 0.00087 (3 seeds against one model). The POD chain gives 0.0275 and 0.00104. A linear head is clearly worse for the β-VAE (0.0450, 0.00176).
6 At $Re = 4\times10^6$, $\alpha = 5^\circ$ the models pick different designs: β-VAE chain m 6.0, p 5.0, t 5.1; POD chain m 6.5, p 4.5, t 5.1; Stage 3 surrogate m 7.0, p 3.5, t 5.1. Every pick lies on the thin edge of the training box (t = 5.09), and the other seeds of each chain pick other cambers, so the ranking near the optimum is not resolved by these models.
7 The predicted polars of both designs agree in shape between the three models inside the training range; maximum $C_L$ 1.79–2.03 and minimum $C_D$ 0.0080–0.0097 depending on model and design.
8 In the five standardised parameters both optima are as close to a training case as a typical test case (distances 0.73 and 0.81; 42nd and 60th percentile of the test cases). In shape alone the Stage 3 surrogate's design is further out (0.53, 96th percentile), and both sit on the thinnest edge of the data.
A1–A3 The β-VAE's test error drops below POD's from epoch 56 and ends at 0.0374; the KL term peaks at 22.0 during the warm-up and settles at 4.45; the pressure error of the fixed case sits at the surface (0.433 within 0.02 chord against 0.032 beyond), largest at the leading edge.
D1 The three chains disagree most where the optima lie: $C_L/C_D$ spread 6.95, 6.75 and 11.69 at the three picks against a grid median of 2.58; 46 candidates lie within one spread of the best ensemble mean (118.1 ± 5.6). On the test cases the spread tracks the error weakly (Spearman 0.29 for $C_L$; the top fifth by spread has 1.5 × the error of the rest).
D2 All 8 latent coordinates are active (std 1.30–2.34 against posterior σ 0.055–0.080). Two follow the angle of attack (correlation +0.90, −0.79) and act as a change of circulation over the whole field; two follow the thickness (+0.80, +0.74); the others mix camber and camber position; none follows $\log_{10} Re$.
D3 0.106 s for 3,600 candidates (0.029 ms each), 20 ms to decode one field, 39 ms from one design to its field, on an Apple M3 Max CPU; latent surrogates trained in 19–38 s, the β-VAE in 73 s. No solver time is assumed.
